item.title: Creative cognition in frontotemporal dementia and brain health.
item.description:
Trends in neurosciences
Creative cognition is central to human thought and is affected by brain disease. Recent findings by Altmayer and colleagues link creative impairment in frontotemporal dementia to rostral prefrontal functional differentiation. These findings motivate a framework for investigating network coordination, circuit physiology, experience-dependent plasticity, and bodily and social regulation in creativity and health.

item.title: When Defense Becomes Compulsion: An Evolutionary and Circuit Framework for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is characterized by intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviors that are frequently organized around preventing potential harm. Although existing neurobiological models have focused on abnormalities in cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits, habit formation, and cognitive control, they provide a less complete explanation for why compulsions preferentially take the form of precautionary actions. Here, we propose an evolutionary and circuit-level framework in which compulsive behavior is understood as a pathological dysregulation of neural systems that normally support adaptive defense. Integrating evidence from human studies with circuit-level findings from rodent studies, we organize defensive control into three sequential but interacting stages: threat appraisal, defensive action selection and execution, and post-defense safety assessment. During threat appraisal, abnormalities in sensory salience, threat valuation, contextual gating, and interoceptive processing may increase the salience or threat value of ambiguous cues. During action selection and execution, intolerance of uncertainty, impaired behavioral flexibility, corticostriatal dysfunction, and negative reinforcement may bias behavior toward premature and repetitive threat-reducing actions that can become increasingly habitual. Following defensive action, impaired outcome evaluation and safety-state updating may prevent successful actions from generating stable signals of safety or completion, allowing defensive responding to persist despite objective threat reduction. By organizing OCD-related circuitry according to when it contributes to defensive processing rather than solely where abnormalities occur, this framework integrates threat-based, corticostriatal, habit, and safety-learning accounts into a process-based model of how adaptive defense may transition into persistent compulsive behavior. This framework may help map stage-specific dysfunction onto symptom heterogeneity and guide more targeted interventions.

item.title: The Separation-Distress Network as a Transdiagnostic Mechanism Linking Relational Adversity, Social Pain, and Psychopathology.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Relational trauma is a major contributor to the development of mental health disorders. This association likely reflects the social nature of humans and other mammals, whose survival depends on maintaining stable social bonds. When these bonds are threatened or disrupted, individuals experience social pain, a distress response mediated by the mammalian separation-distress network. During early development, this network is sensitive to maintaining proximity with caregivers, as independent survival is not yet possible. Converging evidence from ethology, psychodynamic and attachment theory, and social and affective neuroscience supports the function of this network. Because mammalian brains are inherently tuned to form social bonds, adverse relational experiences can disrupt socioemotional development and increase vulnerability to psychopathology. Neural substrates of separation distress include the anterior cingulate cortex, ventral septum, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, dorsal preoptic area, dorsomedial thalamus, and periaqueductal gray, with endogenous opioids and glucocorticoids serving as key neurochemical modulators in the separation-distress response. Separation distress and adverse relational experiences also alter physiological systems implicated in psychopathology, including the HPA axis, autonomic nervous system activity, inflammation, and brain structure and connectivity. This paper argues that relational trauma and social pain are mediated by an evolutionarily conserved subcortical separation-distress network shared across predominantly mammalian species. Dysregulation of this network may represent one common mechanism underlying depression, social anxiety, suicidality, substance use disorders, borderline personality disorder, and other psychiatric conditions. Understanding the processes linking adverse relational experiences, separation-distress activation, and social pain may provide insights into the etiology and treatment of diverse disorders.

item.title: Network disruption in post-stroke depressive symptoms: a Bayesian multicohort study.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Post-stroke depressive symptoms are common, but studies on the contributions of lesion locations to depression symptoms remain inconsistent. Bayesian statistics offer the possibility to clarify these inconsistencies by providing evidence in favor and against observed associations. We reanalyzed four previously published observational cohorts with 1,864 patients with stroke characterized for depressive symptoms from France, Korea, Germany and the USA. We performed voxel-wise Bayes factor mapping using general linear models. Lesion maps were used to test for associations of post-stroke depressive symptoms with lesion location. Network level associations were tested based on structural disconnection and functional lesion network maps estimated by reference to normative connectome data. Due to a sample size with broad lesion coverage, Bayesian inference was informative in large parts of the brain. Lesion associations were found in clusters in the right hemisphere including cortical (frontal, insular, parietal) and subcortical regions (striatum, amygdala, hippocampus) and adjacent white matter. Evidence of no contribution to post-stroke depressive symptoms was observed in large parts of the left hemisphere. Structural disconnection was linked to depressive symptoms in the bilateral frontal white matter prominently involving the corpus callosum and anterior thalamic radiation. Lesion network mapping revealed evidence of an association of post-stroke depressive symptoms with network connectivity in the left posterior cingulate cortex and precuneus, and less consistently, the bilateral anterior insula, along with widespread absence of associations in other regions. Depressive symptoms were most strongly associated with right frontal lesions and right-dominant structural disconnection in frontal cortico-subcortical circuits.

item.title: Brain-heart decoupling in somatic depression: Desynchronization between salience network neuropsychological connectivity and heart rate variability.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Somatic depression is a distinct subtype of major depressive disorder, with a poorer response to treatment, an elevated risk of suicidal behaviour, and a worse prognosis. Interoception, the sense of internal bodily signals, is related to somatic symptoms. However, the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms of body brain communication remain unclear. 293 depressed patients (145 with somatic symptoms and 148 without), and 160 healthy controls underwent magnetoencephalography during a resting state. Both the intra- and inter-network neural oscillation patterns of the salience network, were computed, alongside and heart rate variability (HRV) as a measure of autonomic function. Individuals with somatic depression exhibited lower HRV, accompanied by theta hyper-connectivity within the salience network. Although higher theta connectivity was linked to increased HRV in controls, this correlation was attenuated or even reversed in patients with somatic depression. Our findings identify a specific pattern of brain-heart decoupling in somatic depression, characterized by disrupted communication between salience network theta oscillations and autonomic cardiac regulation. This provides novel neuroimaging evidence for body-brain communication deficits in a clinically important depression subtype.

item.title: Mapping Individual Brain Deviations in ICD-11 Catatonia: Normative Modeling of Structural and Functional MRI Across Two Independent Cohorts.
item.description:
The American journal of psychiatry
Catatonia is a transdiagnostic psychomotor syndrome cutting across mood disorders (MODs) and schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSDs). However, its neurobiological profiles remain poorly characterized. The authors examined structural and resting-state functional normative deviations associated with catatonia across two independent clinical cohorts, using hierarchical Bayesian normative modeling. Structural and resting-state functional MRI data were analyzed from two independent deeply phenotyped cohorts of 280 patients with MODs and SSDs. The Mannheim (Germany) sample included 184 patients with MODs or SSDs (58 with ICD-11 catatonia), and the Bern (Switzerland) sample comprised 96 SSD patients (59 with ICD-11 catatonia). Individual deviations from normative models were estimated using the PCNToolkit, based on healthy reference datasets (N=57,000 structural; N=22,000 functional). Catatonia diagnosis was associated with significant ventricular enlargement (third ventricle and left and right lateral ventricles; q<0.05) and cortical thinning in the left dorsal posterior cingulate and insular cortices (q<0.05) across both cohorts. Exploratory analyses identified a significant left orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) difference between MOD and SSD patients with catatonia. In the overall catatonia versus non-catatonia comparison, the OFC association survived false discovery rate correction only in models adjusted for demographic variables. Resting-state functional analyses showed reduced connectivity between sensorimotor, salience, limbic, and executive control networks at the nominal significance level, but did not survive correction for multiple comparisons. In the combined sample, catatonia was characterized by ventricular enlargement and cingulo-insular cortical thinning, supporting a transdiagnostic model implicating distributed motor-salience integration circuits. These findings provide reproducible, individual-level evidence for distributed brain network involvement in catatonia and identify candidate regions for future mechanistic and neuromodulation studies.

item.title: Opposing effects of childhood abuse and neglect on neural performance monitoring.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
The dimensional model of adversity proposes that threat (abuse) and deprivation (neglect) exert distinct effects on neurocognitive development. We tested whether these dimensions show opposing associations with neural indices of performance monitoring in a sample of 782 young adults from the CoScience EEG-Personality Project. Participants completed the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire alongside an Eriksen flanker task while electroencephalography was recorded. Performance monitoring was indexed by the error-related negativity and frontal midline theta activity. Consistent with preregistered hypotheses, abuse and neglect showed opposing associations with both neural measures. Higher abuse was associated with enhanced error-related negativity but not theta power, whereas higher neglect was associated with attenuated error-related negativity and reduced theta power. Exploratory analyses indicated that these associations were moderated by sex, with stronger effects observed in males. These findings are consistent with the distinction between threat- and deprivation-related adversity and suggest that different forms of childhood adversity may be linked to variation in neurocognitive processes underlying cognitive control. However, the cross-sectional and retrospective nature of the measures limits causal inference and may introduce reporting biases.

item.title: A functional connectome identifies vulnerability to cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease progression.
item.description:
Science advances
Identifying the neurobiological basis of cognitive vulnerability is essential for preventing Alzheimer's disease (AD). We derived the Alzheimer's Resilience-Vulnerability Connectome (ARC) by contrasting SuperAgers (SA), an extreme phenotype of preserved late-life memory, with AD using resting-state fMRI. ARC distinguished SA from AD in a discovery cohort (N = 290; AUC = 0.85) and replicated independently (N = 143), involving prefrontal, temporal, and insular networks and associating with brain age. Applied to cognitively unimpaired adults (discovery: N = 818; replication: N = 497), ARC-based subtyping revealed SA-like and AD-like subgroups with comparable baseline cognition but divergent longitudinal trajectories. AD-like individuals exhibited faster cognitive decline, greater amyloid-β accumulation, and higher AD conversion risk. Exploratory GWAS nominated CLYBL and FRMD6 as candidate novel loci associated with the subtype difference. These findings suggest that ARC captures a continuous connectomic dimension of cognitive aging spanning SA, cognitively typical aging, and AD, highlighting the potential of functional connectomic variation for early risk stratification in AD.

item.title: Cannabidiol and fronto-parietal EEG connectivity in autistic children.
item.description:
Cerebral cortex (New York, N.Y. : 1991)
Autistic children often show altered brain network connectivity, including circuitry implicated in social cognition. Cannabidiol (CBD) has emerged as a potential therapy for autism, but its neural mechanisms remain under-researched. Here, we analyze resting-state data collected as part of a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial, to explore whether 12 weeks of oral CBD oil could modulate functional connectivity in autistic children. Twenty-nine autistic children (5 to 12 years) completed two 12-week intervention periods (CBD and placebo, randomized) separated by an 8-week washout. Before and after each period, 5 min of eyes-open resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) were obtained from a subset of 18 participants (8 female). Functional connectivity was calculated across 16 electrode-pairs in the delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands. Beta-band connectivity between the right frontal and right inferior-parietal electrodes increased following CBD (P = 0.001, false discovery rate [FDR]-corrected P [pFDR] = 0.022), and alpha connectivity showed an increase that did not remain following FDR correction (P = 0.036, pFDR = 0.428). No significant differences were observed following placebo for any frequency band (pFDR > 0.69). This study provides preliminary evidence that 12 weeks of cannabidiol is associated with an increase in right fronto-parietal (F4-P8) functional connectivity in autistic children, most pronounced in the beta-band. Replication in larger samples is needed to confirm generalizability and clinical relevance.

item.title: Neurobehavioral correlates of changing one's mind in ADHD and OCD.
item.description:
Cerebral cortex (New York, N.Y. : 1991)
Cognitive flexibility is an executive function that allows individuals to adjust behavior in response to changing environmental demands. We assessed volitional switching under uncertainty, without rule-based learning, in the "Change Your Mind" task. Nineteen patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), 19 patients with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and matched control participants (20 per group) completed the task while undergoing a functional MRI scan. The task was a two-alternative forced choice paradigm where each stimulus was presented twice successively, with spurious feedback following the first presentation. This allowed participants the opportunity to repeat or change their response. Participants with ADHD changed their response more frequently than controls following a previously correct response, associated with reduced accuracy on the second trial. This was accompanied with smaller differences between change and repeat trials in the superior frontal gyrus, paracingulate gyrus, and frontal pole compared to controls. Participants with OCD did not differ from healthy controls in their performance but exhibited greater activity on both change and repeat trials in the pre- and postcentral gyri than controls. These results point to distinct neurobehavioral differences in patients with ADHD and OCD underlying what is often termed more broadly inflexible behavior.

item.title: Aggression in epilepsy and sleep: from historical accounts to brain networks and human behaviour.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
For a long time, epilepsy has been associated with violent behaviour, acquiring a highly stigmatizing reputation, shaped mainly by 19th century medical theories that postulated a direct connection between epilepsy and the criminal personality. Such stigma exerts a negative effect on the quality of life of people with epilepsy and remains a significant concern in forensic settings. This narrative review aims to provide a thorough exploration of the relationship between epilepsy and aggression, highlighting the misconceptions that contribute to this stigma. The evidence presented in this review draws on the authors' experience and a PubMed search conducted in December 2024. The manuscript is organized into five sections, addressing: (i) the historical and cultural background of epilepsy and violence; (ii) the clinical features of aggression as a peri-ictal manifestation; (iii) the neural networks underlying aggression in epilepsy; (iv) aggression in sleep-related disorders, an area closely related to epilepsy, where clinical interest and reports of sleep-related violent episodes have increased progressively in recent years; and (v) forensic considerations. In total, 326 records were identified through the PubMed search. Only papers relevant to the topics were included. Relevant publications were also added manually from the authors' own files. One hundred and thirty-two studies were ultimately included in this narrative review. The review, addressing the topic from a historical perspective, traces the evolution of stigma and the concept of the 'epileptic personality', from early observations to contemporary understanding. Next, we explore aggression and violence as peri-ictal manifestations, examining both their clinical characteristics and the brain networks implicated in the generation of aggressive behaviours during seizures. We try to elucidate the neurobiological substrates underlying these manifestations using intracerebral recordings. We then turn to violence associated with parasomnias, analysing and comparing the mechanisms underlying aggression and violence occurring in epileptic seizures with those observed during sleep in parasomnias, integrating evidence from intracranial EEG studies of disorders of arousal. This comparison highlights key similarities, differences and the risk of a misdiagnosis. Finally, we address the legal and forensic implications of seizure- and sleep-related aggression and violence. Epileptic seizures and parasomnias can cause injuries to the affected person or to those nearby, but they can rarely be truly classified as acts of violence. However, although aggressive behaviour is uncommon during seizures, it may lead to legal consequences. Despite efforts from scientific societies and patient organizations, the stigma of epilepsy persists, requiring further action and a deeper scientific understanding of this subject.

item.title: Dissociating executive prefrontal substrates following capsulotomy in obsessive-compulsive disorder.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is characterized by widespread executive function impairments linked to disrupted frontostriatal circuits. Ablative therapies such as capsulotomy show promising efficacy in treatment-refractory OCD, yet their effects on executive neural substrates remain poorly understood. This study explores how OCD and capsulotomy influence executive prefrontal function. Twenty-three post-capsulotomy OCD patients, 30 OCD controls and 32 health controls (HC) were recruited in the study. Post-capsulotomy patients were recruited at least 6 months following surgery to allow for postoperative stabilization. Participants completed three executive function tasks assessing distinct cognitive domains: the Extra-Dimensional Intra-Dimensional (EDID) task testing set-shifting, the N-back task testing working memory and the Flanker task measuring conflict processing. The EDID and N-back tasks were administered during concurrent task-based functional MRI, while the Flanker task provided only behavioural measures. In the EDID task, OCD capsulotomy patients demonstrated greater post-error flexibility towards ID versus ED shifting relative to both OCD controls and HC, despite exhibiting more ED errors. OCD controls showed less shifts after errors compared with HC, which was not revealed in the capsulotomy group. OCD patients showed less neural differentiation between ED versus ID in lateral and mesial prefrontal regions relative to HC. Capsulotomy was associated with decreased pre-supplementary motor area activity to ED shifts compared with HC, indicating impairments in neural reactivity to ED shifting. No evidence supported the influence of capsulotomy in the N-back or the Flanker tasks. Specifically, both OCD groups showed impaired working memory performance at high memory load along with dysfunction in the whole frontoparietal network. In the Flanker task, impairments in dissociating congruent and incongruent conditions were found in both OCD groups but not in the HC group. These findings suggest capsulotomy specifically remediates error-monitoring and behavioural flexibility through mesial prefrontal remodelling, while leaving working memory and conflict processing deficits intact. This dissociation implies that cognitive flexibility may represent a state-dependent process amenable to intervention, whereas working memory and conflict processing impairments may reflect trait markers of OCD vulnerability. These results have clinical implications on the relative safety profile of capsulotomy and patient selection for precision neuromodulation.

item.title: Blunted response of caudal locus coeruleus to arousing stimuli in Parkinson's disease.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Parkinson's disease (PD) causes progressive degeneration of noradrenergic neurons in the locus coeruleus (LC), contributing to non-motor symptoms. Using neuromelanin-sensitive ultra-high field (7 T) MRI, we previously identified a reduction in neuromelanin signal in the caudal LC, indicating a rostro-caudal gradient of noradrenergic cell loss. Caudal LC degeneration was associated with greater severity of non-motor symptoms such as orthostatic hypotension and apathy. In the current case-control study, we expanded the PD cohort to further corroborate the structure-symptom relationships within the LC and investigate how degeneration along the rostro-caudal LC axis affects arousal-related functional responsivity. To this end, 71 people with PD in the ON-medication state and 40 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent clinical assessments and 7 T magnetization transfer-weighted (MTw) MRI to quantify structural changes along the rostro-caudal LC axis. A subgroup of 30 people with PD and 27 controls underwent 7 T functional MRI to assess LC responsivity to arousing auditory and visual stimuli in two functional MRI sessions on separate days. Healthy controls were scanned twice without medication, while people with PD were studied on and off dopaminergic medication in counterbalanced order. In the PD group, MTw MRI confirmed a significant reduction of the regional neuromelanin signal in the caudal LC relative to the control group (P = 0.010). This structural disintegration correlated with orthostatic hypotension (P = 0.009) and cognitive impairment (P = 0.036), corroborating its clinical relevance. Functional MRI revealed reduced activation of the caudal LC to arousing visual and auditory stimuli in people with PD relative to controls (P = 0.012). This difference reached statistical significance only in the ON-medication state, with a similar but non-significant trend in the OFF-medication state (P = 0.105). In an exploratory analysis of a smaller subsample, structural and functional caudal LC signals were significantly correlated in both people with PD and healthy controls (P = 0.007). Together, the findings provide evidence for a rostro-caudal gradient of LC pathology in PD at both structural and functional levels. While structural MRI provides fine-grained insights into spatial gradients of disease-related pathology, functional MRI captures the impaired functional responsivity of the caudal LC. The presence of arousal-induced hypoactivation of the caudal LC in the ON-medication state indicates that LC dysfunction extends beyond dopamine deficits in PD, highlighting complex interactions between dopaminergic and noradrenergic systems.

item.title: Behavioural rigidity as a transdiagnostic marker of nucleus accumbens dysfunction in dementia.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Behavioural rigidity, the tendency to persist with inflexible patterns of thoughts or actions, is increasingly recognized as a transdiagnostic symptom across psychiatric, neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders. Empirical studies exploring the prevalence and underlying neural mechanisms of behavioural rigidity in dementia, however, are lacking. This cross-sectional study sought to delineate the structural and functional neural correlates of behavioural rigidity using a transdiagnostic approach looking across the frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) spectrum and Alzheimer's disease (AD). A total of 204 participants were recruited, including 110 frontotemporal dementia (FTD), 53 AD and 41 healthy older control participants. Within the FTD group, 66 cases were diagnosed with clinically probable behavioural variant FTD (bvFTD), 26 presented with semantic dementia (SD) and 18 cases had progressive non-fluent aphasia (PNFA). Behavioural rigidity was assessed using the Stereotypical and Motor Behaviour subscale of the Cambridge Behavioural Inventory-Revised. Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) was performed to identify grey matter regions associated with behavioural rigidity transdiagnostically, the results of which informed subsequent seed-based voxel-wise functional connectivity analyses. All imaging analyses were adjusted for relevant demographic and technical covariates. Statistical thresholds were set at voxel-level P < 0.001 (uncorrected) and cluster-level P < 0.05 (false discovery rate corrected). Our main finding was that behavioural rigidity is pervasive across dementia subtypes, ranging from most pronounced in bvFTD to milder/relatively absent in PNFA, relative to controls. Whole-brain VBM across the entire patient sample revealed a significant negative association between behavioural rigidity and grey matter intensity exclusively in the bilateral nucleus accumbens. Using the bilateral nucleus accumbens as seeds, resting-state functional connectivity analysis showed that higher levels of behavioural rigidity were associated with stronger connectivity between the left nucleus accumbens and the left supplementary motor area, paracentral lobule and precuneus. This is the first study, to our knowledge, to examine the neural substrates of behavioural rigidity across FTLD syndromes transdiagnostically using structural and functional neuroimaging approaches. Our findings reveal a gradation of rigid and repetitive behaviours, most apparent in bvFTD, which in turn reflects pathological disruption of the nucleus accumbens. Taken together, our findings highlight the need to consider repetitive and rigid behaviours as a transdiagnostic feature in neurodegenerative disorders, and one which indexes underlying nucleus accumbens pathology. More broadly, this study underscores the importance of screening for rigid and repetitive behaviours in the clinic and identifies the nucleus accumbens as a promising neural target to ameliorate these symptoms.

item.title: Mapping cerebellar morphology in 15q11.2 CNV carriers using normative modeling.
item.description:
Molecular psychiatry
Copy number variations (CNVs) at the 15q11.2 locus of the human genome have been associated with altered brain structure and increased risk for neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders. The cerebellum is increasingly seen as a crucial brain region for neurodevelopmental conditions, yet the effects of 15q11.2 CNVs on cerebellar morphology remain largely unclear. Importantly, 15q11.2 CNVs shows reduced or incomplete penetrance (meaning that not all CNV carriers are affected) and variable expressivity (meaning that symptoms may differ between individuals with the same genetic alteration). Thus, there is a need to not only assess group differences, but also to quantify anatomical variability at the individual level. Here, we address these issues using normative models of brain anatomy trained on large datasets (n > 52k, age range: 3-85) to assess both group and individual-level deviations in cerebellar anatomy in carriers of 15q11.2 deletions (n = 120, mean [SD] age = 64.95 [7.58]) and duplications (n = 149, mean [SD] age = 64.31 [7.21]), compared to non-carriers (n = 19,028, mean [SD] age = 64.31 [7.58]). Group-level case-control analyses revealed significantly smaller total and regional cerebellar volumes in both deletion and duplication carriers, though with small effect sizes. Individual-level deviation analyses, capturing pronounced alterations in specific individuals, revealed a heterogeneous pattern among carriers. Overall, our findings suggest that CNVs at the 15q11.2 locus exert modest and highly individualized effects on cerebellar morphology.

item.title: The Red Nucleus in Motor Control and Autism Spectrum Disorder.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Neuromotor differences of motor coordination, timing, postural regulation, and prospective motor control are common and emerge early in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). However, their underlying neural mechanisms remain incompletely understood, with existing research emphasising cortical and cerebellar systems. This review re-examines the red nucleus (RN), a midbrain structure embedded within cortical, cerebellar, and olivary motor pathways, as an underexplored component of distributed sensorimotor networks. We synthesise evidence from comparative neuroanatomy, animal experiments, human neuroimaging, movement disorders, and autism research, distinguishing direct RN findings from broader circuit-level inferences. Neuroimaging studies have reported RN-region susceptibility differences in autistic children, including an exploratory association with fine-motor development, but reproducible links to specific motor processes and RN-related causal mechanisms remain unestablished. We therefore propose a testable hypothesis that differences in RN structure, function, or connectivity may be associated with specific dimensions of motor function in autism. Error-related sensorimotor adaptation provides a primary experimental target, complemented by prospective motor control. Future investigations combining RN-sensitive neuroimaging, quantitative motor assessment, and transdiagnostic comparisons with developmental coordination disorder may determine whether RN-related measures provide explanatory information beyond sensorimotor systems. This framework positions the RN as a candidate component of autism-related motor networks.

item.title: A Dynamic Model of Amygdala Circuits in Threat and Reward: Implications for Affective Disorders.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Animals must continuously evaluate their surroundings and select adaptive responses to survive in ever-changing environments. Central to this capacity is the assignment of importance to environmental cues, which guides motivated behavior toward rewarding opportunities and away from potential threats. Here we propose a theoretical framework, a dynamic motivational model based on threat and reward imminence, in which motivational states evolve continuously as a function of imminence rather than shifting between discrete stages. Within this framework, three interacting dimensions define the stimulus relevance of an environmental cue: salience, valence, and value. We leverage the amygdala as a substrate to illustrate the circuit mechanisms underlying importance assignment and examine how stimulus imminence drives motivational state transitions to promote adaptive behavior. Applied to affective disorders, it reframes amygdala dysfunction as projection- and circuit-specific stress adaptation rather than uniform regional hyperactivity, providing a common language for comparing major depressive disorder, anxiety disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder, and substance use disorders. By integrating animal circuit studies with human neuroimaging and clinical evidence, this framework positions amygdala-centered networks as candidate biomarkers for biologically informed subtyping and targets for personalized treatment in depression and related affective disorders.

item.title: Age-dependent structural brain aging in medication-free major depressive disorder: A multi-site analysis from COORDINATE-MDD consortium.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Major depressive disorder (MDD) is associated with altered brain structure and accelerated brain aging. However, previous studies have been limited by clinical samples with mixed medication status and multiple mood states, modest sample sizes, underrepresentation of older adults with MDD, and/or reliance on summary-level data. Harmonized T1-weighted MRI from MDD (n = 645), all medication-free and in a current depressive episode, and matched healthy controls (n = 645), segmented into 145 regional volumes, from 11 sites in COORDINATE-MDD consortium. Brain age gap (BAG) was estimated cross-sectionally using gradient boosting regression with nested cross-validation. Group differences in BAG (and age-corrected BAG [cBAG]) were examined across age strata. Regional contributions were evaluated using SHAP values. MDD was associated with significantly elevated cBAG compared with healthy controls (mean difference + 2.0 years [95% CI 1.251, 2.774], Cohen's d -0.289 [95% CI -0.399, -0.179]). Age-stratified analyses showed no differences before mid-30s, with progressively larger gaps thereafter, reaching +6.8 years in MDD aged 55 and older in unadjusted analyses (4.3 years after accounting for site). cBAG differed across neuroanatomical phenotypes previously identified using COORDINATE-MDD data. Key contributing regions included lateral and medial prefrontal regions, middle temporal gyrus, putamen, supplementary motor cortex, central operculum, and cerebellum. Structural brain aging in MDD is age-dependent and most pronounced in a neuroanatomical phenotype associated with poorer key clinical outcomes. The findings are consistent with, but do not establish, neuroprogression models of MDD and demonstrate that cBAG is not a uniform feature of MDD, being more strongly expressed in a specifically clinically vulnerable disease phenotype.

item.title: Negative emotion recognition impairments despite preserved neural activity in patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI).
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Emotion recognition is an essential component of socio-emotional functioning, yet its alteration in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) remains insufficiently understood, particularly in relation to neural mechanisms. This study examined behavioral and neural responses to facial emotions in 60 adults (30 MCI, 30 healthy controls (HC)) using a validated fMRI emotion-recognition paradigm with anger, fear, sadness, happiness, and neutral expressions. Although groups did not differ in overall recognition accuracy, a multivariate analysis revealed a significant group effect driven by a selective impairment in sadness recognition in MCI. Accuracy for anger and fear showed weaker, but non-significant differences between groups, and happiness recognition was preserved. Face-processing ability, emotional interference, emotional intelligence, and domain-specific cognitive performance showed no significant associations with facial emotion recognition, indicating that the sadness-specific deficit was not attributable to perceptual, cognitive, or socio-emotional characteristics. In fMRI analyses, HCs showed widespread activation to emotional versus neutral faces across occipital, frontal, and subcortical regions, whereas patients with MCI exhibited spatially more restricted activation. However, whole-brain group comparisons revealed no significant differences in BOLD response amplitudes for overall emotion processing or any emotion-specific contrast. These findings indicate that MCI is characterized by a selective impairment in recognizing sadness, an emotion relying on subtle, low-intensity cues, while whole-brain analyses did not reveal statistically significant group differences in neural responses during emotion processing. This pattern shows that group differences in behavior did not correspond to group differences in measured neural activity.

item.title: Transcranial magnetic stimulation to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex modulates single-neuron activity in humans.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) is an established treatment for depression, yet the fundamental question of how cortical stimulation influences single neurons in deep brain circuits critical for mood regulation remains unanswered. Using a rare opportunity to record from intracranial microelectrodes while TMS was delivered in four neurosurgical patients, we evaluated the responses of 185 single neurons. Artifact cleaning enabled single-neuron spikes to be resolved as early as 8 ms after stimulation. We found that single-pulse TMS to the left dlPFC elicited time-locked firing responses in 46% of neurons (26% facilitated only, 19% suppressed only, 1% both). These responses occurred within deep bilateral cortical and subcortical structures, including the putamen and thalamus. Single-pulse TMS tended to facilitate spiking in striato-thalamic putative inhibitory neurons from ~8 ms, peaking at ~80 to 100 ms, and decaying until ~600 ms. In contrast, putative excitatory neurons and limbic areas were suppressed with a slower time course lasting to ~1,000 ms. TMS-evoked potentials recorded from intracranial depth macroelectrodes to quantify network activity revealed that the modulation of responsive neurons was positively correlated with cortico-striato-thalamic network activity and anticorrelated with limbic network activity in one participant with sufficient network and unit sampling. These results suggest that dlPFC TMS recruits a high percentage of neurons spanning cortical and subcortical brain regions bilaterally. The recruitment pattern selectively involves increasing the firing rate of inhibitory neurons in executive control networks while suppressing limbic excitatory drive, providing a candidate cellular mechanism for how cortical stimulation modulates distributed brain networks.

item.title: Distinct Patterns of Syntactic Errors Doubly Dissociate in Chronic Poststroke Aphasia.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
The lesion correlates of syntactic deficits in aphasia remain poorly understood. Previous studies have suggested that distinct error types in expressive syntax may be associated with damage to different brain regions, but the specific lesion correlates of these errors have not been fully delineated. To address this gap, we analyzed spontaneous speech samples from individuals with chronic aphasia, categorizing errors into hierarchical (paragrammatic-like) and linearization (agrammatic-like) errors. Lesion-symptom mapping was conducted to identify brain regions associated with these error types. Lesion clusters in the medial superior temporal sulcus and inferior parietal lobe were associated with hierarchical errors, whereas frontal lesions, including those in the inferior and middle frontal lobe, were associated with linearization errors. These results provide support for a two-stage model of syntactic encoding, with distinct neural correlates for hierarchical and linearization processes. Our findings suggest that distinct brain regions contribute to different stages of syntactic encoding. Hierarchical processing seems to be supported by posterior temporal-parietal regions, whereas linearization seems to be supported by frontal regions. These results suggest that the diagnosis and treatment of aphasia could take into account the existence of distinct syntactic production deficits resulting from different patterns of brain damage.

item.title: Diagnostic and sex effects on frontostriatal brain wiring structural organization in early psychosis affective subjects compared to healthy controls.
item.description:
Molecular psychiatry
Background Brain connectivity abnormalities may underlie affective psychosis which may be influenced by sex. Using diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) tractography, we assessed frontostriatal brain wiring connectivity patterns in 46 early psychosis affective and 56 healthy control young adult, male and female participants. Methods We collected harmonized whole brain tractography dMRI data from three sites and applied our novel fiber clustering methodology to identify 17 white matter fiber clusters connecting the frontal cortex and caudate per hemisphere in each group. By comparing cortical and caudate inter-cluster endpoint distances between groups, we assessed their patterns of frontostriatal connectivity. Results 1) In both males and females in early affective psychosis and healthy controls, bilaterally, the frontal cortex to caudate wiring pattern deviated from a topographic organization. 2) in a right hemisphere frontal pole fiber cluster, independent of sex, we found a significant interaction effect of diagnosis on the connectivity pattern between frontal cortex and caudate, (p = 0.013); 3) in a left hemisphere inferior frontal gyrus, pars triangularis, fiber cluster, we found sex influenced the significant interaction effect of diagnosis on the connectivity pattern between frontal cortex and caudate, (p = 0.0085), with the effect much greater in females (p < 0.00001) than in males (p = 0.97); and, 4) post-hoc tests showed a significant effect of diagnosis on the pattern of frontal cortex to caudate connectivity in specific subregions (ps ≤0.04). Conclusions Importantly, while the frontostriatal wiring pattern in both early affective psychosis and healthy controls deviated from a topographic organization, we found in a right hemisphere fiber cluster, independent of sex, that a significant interaction effect of diagnosis was observed on the frontal cortex to caudate connectivity pattern, whereas, in a left hemisphere fiber cluster, the effect of diagnosis on connectivity pattern was influenced by sex, showing the importance of the role of sex in brain wiring patterns in early affective psychosis.

item.title: SPARK-ICA: Guided Frequency-Resolved Dynamic Spatial ICA Reveals Fine-Scale fMRI Network Dynamics.
item.description:
Human brain mapping
Fine-scale spatiotemporal dynamics of functional brain networks are increasingly recognized as critical markers of transient connectivity and neuropsychiatric pathology. However, many existing dynamic fMRI methods primarily focus on temporal variability without explicitly resolving the spatial-frequency content of network dynamics, potentially limiting characterization of subtle, high-frequency spatial reconfigurations. To address this gap, we propose SPARK-ICA (Spatial-frequency Partitioned, Adaptive Reconstruction using Knowledge-guided ICA), a frequency-resolved dynamic spatial independent component analysis (ICA) framework that integrates NeuroMark template guidance with spatial frequency decomposition and group-level ICA of time-resolved, band-specific spatial maps. Starting from template-guided NeuroMark networks, we first estimate time-varying spatial maps using a dynamic guided ICA approach, capturing subject-specific network expression over time. Each dynamic spatial map is then decomposed into multiple spatial frequency bands using Fourier-domain spatial filtering, isolating fine- to coarse-scale spatial features at each time point. Band-specific spatial maps are subsequently concatenated and subjected to a blind group-level multi-frequency ICA, yielding a compact latent representation in which each dynamic component is characterized by distinct spatial-frequency signatures. These group-level band-resolved components are then used as references to estimate subject- and band-specific time courses and maps via spatially constrained ICA, enabling frequency-specific analysis of both long-term correlations and short-term temporal variability while preserving reproducibility across subjects. Using resting-state fMRI data from schizophrenia (SZ) patients and healthy controls (HC), we evaluated both long-term correlations and short-term variability of band-resolved dynamic time courses. For the group-level analyses, we focused on a predefined subset of NeuroMark networks with well-established involvement in SZ-related dysconnectivity. Our results reveal frequency-specific abnormalities in SZ, with enhanced long-term connectivity within sensory and subcortical networks and pronounced short-term alterations involving predominantly higher-frequency spatial components, particularly in cerebellar and subcortical systems. These findings indicate that SZ-related dysregulation is differentially expressed across spatial-frequency and temporal scales, rather than reflecting uniform dysconnectivity. Together, this framework provides a unified approach for analyzing dynamic fMRI networks across spatial, temporal, and frequency dimensions, extending our previous NeuroMark-DyFICA framework from a predominantly high-frequency spatial representation to an explicitly frequency-resolved characterization of dynamic network organization. By explicitly modeling spatial frequency-dependent dynamics, the proposed method provides a more resolved characterization of network alterations and offers a framework for identifying candidate markers of neuropsychiatric disorders.

item.title: Neural Markers of Reward Valuation and Impulsive Decision-Making in Mania Risk.
item.description:
JAMA psychiatry
IMPORTANCE: Mania or hypomania, the pathognomonic feature of bipolar disorder (BD), is associated with reward hypersensitivity and impulsive decision-making, but the neural mechanisms underlying these distinct behavioral facets remain unclear. Reward expectancy (RE)-associated activation in the left ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (L-vlPFC) and pre-supplementary motor area (pre-SMA) is elevated in individuals at risk of mania or hypomania, but it is unknown whether elevated activation in these regions and associations with risk-related behavioral facets reflect convergent or dissociable pathways to mania or hypomania risk or whether depression severity impacts these associations. OBJECTIVE: To test whether RE-associated L-vlPFC and pre-SMA activation exhibit distinct associations with delay discounting behavior-indexing reward valuation (lower discounting) vs impulsive decision-making (higher discounting)-and whether these associations are moderated by depression severity. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: In this cross-sectional study, 2 independent samples of adults aged approximately 18 to 30 years at varying risk of mania or hypomania (142 in the discovery set and 86 in the replication set) completed a functional magnetic resonance imaging reward task and a delay discounting assessment. Major exclusion criteria included current or lifetime BD, primary psychotic disorders, neurological disorders, recent substance use disorders, systemic medical illnesses, and magnetic resonance imaging contraindications. The study took place from 2019 to 2026 at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. EXPOSURE: RE-associated L-vlPFC and pre-SMA activation. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Main outcomes were mania or hypomania risk per Mood Spectrum Self-Report-Lifetime mania score and delay discounting behavior per 27-Item Monetary Choice Questionnaire rate. Associations were tested using regression models, including moderation by depression severity. RESULTS: Across 228 individuals (discovery: mean [SD] age, 23.79 [3.32] years; 96 [67.6%] female; replication: mean [SD] age, 26.09 [3.15] years; 64 [74.4%] female), L-vlPFC and pre-SMA activation were both positively associated with mania or hypomania risk in the discovery sample (l-vlPFC: β, 0.544; 95% CI, 0.440 to 0.649; z, 10.24; P < .001 and pre-SMA: β, 0.496; 95% CI, 0.341 to 0.650; z, 6.30; P < .001) and replication sample (l-vlPFC: β, 0.503; 95% CI, 0.241 to 0.765; z, 3.77; P < .001 and pre-SMA: β, 0.684; 95% CI, 0.410 to 0.957; z, 4.90; P < .001). In the discovery sample, these regions showed dissociable delay discounting associations: greater L-vlPFC activation was associated with lower discounting (β, -0.305; 95% CI, -0.561 to -0.050; P = .02), whereas greater pre-SMA activation was associated with higher discounting (β, 0.521; 95% CI, 0.146 to 0.895; P = .007). The L-vlPFC-lower discounting association replicated (β, -0.704; 95% CI, -1.400 to -0.008; P = .048). A pre-SMA activation × depression severity interaction was observed in the replication sample (β, -0.427; 95% CI, -0.792 to -0.063; P = .02), such that higher depression severity attenuated the association between elevated pre-SMA activation and higher discounting. This interaction was detectable in the discovery sample in individuals with elevated pre-SMA activation (β, -0.285; 95% CI, -0.565 to -0.005; t63 = -2.03; P = .046). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: The findings in this cross-sectional study suggest that RE-associated L-vlPFC and pre-SMA activation may represent dissociable neural pathways to mania or hypomania risk. Elevated L-vlPFC activation was associated with sensitivity to reward value, whereas elevated pre-SMA activation was associated with impulsive decision-making, and this latter association was moderated by depression severity.

item.title: Neural and cognitive correlates of adolescent anxiety: Widespread brain network alterations, increased control costs, and visuospatial processing deficits.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
This study investigated the neural substrates and cognitive correlates of adolescent anxiety, which are currently incompletely understood, in N = 3,499 youth with median (IQR) age 12.0 (1.1) years (~51.0% females), from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Study. Resting-state fMRI, structural MRI, anxiety (scores and related disorder diagnoses), and neurocognitive data were analyzed. Mixed-effects regression models were used to examine associations between anxiety, brain characteristics (topological and morphometric properties, and regulatory (control) costs of intrinsic network dynamics), and cognitive outcomes. Females, older youth, and those with more parental mental health problems had higher anxiety (β = 0.04-1.15, 95% CI = [0.01, 2.18]). Higher resting-state connectivity and/or centrality (network importance) of the cerebellum, amygdala, and thalamus, and higher cerebellum-basal-ganglia-thalamus control costs were associated with higher anxiety (β = 0.04-0.08, 95% CI = [0.01, 0.11]). In contrast, temporoparietal and frontoparietal network efficiency and resilience (robustness) were protective for social and/or generalized anxiety disorders (adjusted odds ratio (aOR) = 0.72-0.80, 95% CI = [0.62, 0.98]). Higher cortical thickness and/or volume of the superior temporal gyrus, pars opercularis, precentral gyrus, and putamen were associated with higher odds of generalized or social anxiety disorder (aOR = 1.28-1.44, 95% CI = [1.07, 1.78]). Finally, anxiety was associated with lower response accuracy in the Little Man Task (β = -0.05, 95% CI = [-0.09, -0.01]), and attenuated positive brain-task performance associations. These findings suggest that adolescent anxiety is associated with widespread brain alterations, especially in the cerebellum-basal ganglia-thalamus network, while the organization of frontoparietal and temporoparietal networks, which play as key role in emotion regulation and social function, is protective for anxiety disorders. It is also associated with lower visuospatial processing and alterations in the networks that support it.

item.title: Brain systems supporting the narrative self and psychopathology.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Disturbances in the narrative self are implicated across psychiatric disorders, with abnormalities in the neural systems supporting its generation and regulation constituting a transdiagnostic risk factor for mental illness. This review highlights how alterations in these brain systems underlie prevalent clinical features, including diminished, rigid, and sustained negative beliefs within the narrative self. The narrative self is framed as a higher-order construct that emerges from multiple systems, with reward, punishment, and motivational signals biasing which experiences are encoded as self-defining and which self-beliefs are reinforced over time. We discuss recent evidence demonstrating how the narrative self is supported by distributed brain networks in which subcortical inputs from the basal forebrain, habenula and mediodorsal thalamus modulate default mode network activity, with the salience, frontoparietal, cingulo-opercular, and hippocampal-parahippocampal networks regulating how self-beliefs are established or updated. Adolescence is emphasized as a developmental period uniquely vulnerable to disturbances in the formation of a coherent, flexible narrative self, wherein asynchronous subcortical and cortical development and pubertal changes interact to confer risk for diminished and rigid self-beliefs. Belief-updating tasks, hierarchical computational models, and ecological momentary assessment are proposed as approaches to quantify how self-beliefs form and shift across time, linking neural signatures of the narrative self to momentary variability. We propose that treating the narrative self as a primary level of explanation for psychopathology positions it as a testable target for future neuroimaging research, providing a clearer bridge from self-referential cognition to interventions in daily life.
